final_answer: >>> mRNA vaccines work by delivering a piece of genetic material called messenger RNA (mRNA) into the body. This mRNA contains instructions for cells to produce a harmless piece of the virus, typically a protein like the spike protein found on the surface of the virus. Once the mRNA is inside the body, it is taken up by cells, which then use the mRNA to produce the viral protein. The protein is then displayed on the surface of the cells, which alerts the immune system to the presence of a foreign substance. The immune system responds by producing antibodies and activating T-cells to attack the protein. These immune responses create memory cells that remember how to fight the virus if it is encountered in the future. Importantly, the mRNA does not enter the nucleus of the cell and does not alter the DNA, making it a safe and effective way to trigger an immune response without causing disease.
